title: Faraday's laws
examples: How do I calculate the mass deposited if I know the moles of electrons?
What is the relationship between current, time, and moles of electrons?
Can you explain the difference between moles of electrons and moles of substance?

explain.say: Today we are learning about Faraday's laws in electrochemistry.

items: Faraday's laws relate electricity to chemical changes.
They help us calculate amounts deposited at electrodes.
The key unit for calculation is moles of electrons.

explain.say: The first law states that the mass deposited is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.
The second law states that the mass deposited depends on the chemical reaction involved.
We must always use the concept of moles of electrons for calculations.
If you know the moles of electrons, you use the mole ratio from the half-reaction.
In a real battery, the total charge passed determines the total metal deposited.

faq.q: What is the Faraday constant, and why do I need it?
faq.a: The Faraday constant is the charge carried by one mole of electrons. It is approximately 96,500 coulombs. You need it to convert the total charge passed, measured in coulombs, into moles of electrons.
asks: What is the value of F?
How do I use the Faraday constant?

faq.q: Do I use the mass of the metal or the moles of electrons in the final calculation?
faq.a: You must use the moles of electrons first. You calculate the moles of electrons from the charge, and then use the balanced half-reaction to find the moles of metal deposited.
asks: Should I use grams or moles at the end?

faq.q: Does the type of metal change how I calculate the moles of electrons?
faq.a: No, the moles of electrons calculation depends only on the total charge passed. The metal type only affects the mole ratio in the half-reaction.
asks: Is the charge the same for all metals?
Does the metal affect the charge calculation?

faq.q: If the current changes, do I recalculate the moles of electrons every time?
faq.a: Yes, if the current changes, you must recalculate the total charge passed, and thus the moles of electrons, for that specific time interval.
asks: What if the current is not constant?
Do I integrate if the current changes?

faq.q: Is the mass deposited directly proportional to the current?
faq.a: No, it is proportional to the product of the current and the time. The relationship is linear with charge, not just current.
asks: Is it just about the current strength?

facts: Faraday's laws link electrical current to chemical deposition.
The quantity of electricity is measured in coulombs.
One mole of electrons carries a charge of approximately 96,500 coulombs.
The stoichiometry of the half-reaction determines the mole ratio.

quiz.say: A cell passes 1.0 mole of electrons. If the deposition reaction is $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Cu}$, what is the moles of copper deposited?
quiz.why: The balanced equation shows two moles of electrons are needed for one mole of copper, so the ratio is 2:1.

wrong.0: This incorrectly assumes that the moles of electrons are multiplied by the stoichiometry coefficient.
wrong.1: This incorrectly calculates the ratio by dividing the moles of electrons by the charge.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes a one-to-one mole ratio between electrons and metal.

quiz.say: If the total charge passed is 193,000 coulombs, how many moles of electrons were passed?
quiz.why: You divide the total charge passed by the Faraday constant to get the moles of electrons.

wrong.0: This incorrectly multiplies the charge by the Faraday constant.
wrong.2: This incorrectly treats the Faraday constant as a simple multiplier instead of a divisor.
wrong.3: This confuses the constant value with the calculated amount.

quiz.say: For the reaction $\text{Ag}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Ag}$, if 0.5 moles of electrons pass, what is the moles of silver deposited?
quiz.why: The balanced half-reaction shows a direct one-to-one ratio between electrons and silver atoms.

wrong.0: This incorrectly assumes a 2:1 ratio based on common textbook examples.
wrong.1: This incorrectly assumes that the moles of electrons are multiplied by two.
wrong.2: This is a common mistake that divides the moles of electrons by two unnecessarily.
